title: Types of economic systems and economic resources — 1.2

blocks.heading: Resources and allocation are different questions
blocks.text: The factors of production describe the contributions that make production possible. Land supplies natural resources, labour supplies human effort, capital supplies produced productive assets and entrepreneurship organises the venture while bearing business risk. An invented vegetable grower near Otjiwarongo uses soil and water, workers, irrigation equipment and decisions about what to grow and how to market it. These categories answer a different question from whether the business is privately or publicly owned. A government-owned enterprise can use the same four factors as a privately owned producer. A factory may also be described by its manufacturing activity without that description identifying its owner. Classifying the contribution carefully prevents money, machines, natural resources and management effort from being treated as interchangeable. Several contributions can be supplied by the same person or organisation.

blocks.heading: Ask what, how and for whom
blocks.text: An economy has to coordinate what goods and services are produced, how resources are combined and who receives the resulting output. A market system gives prices and decisions by buyers and sellers the main coordinating role. If customers are willing and able to buy a product, the prospect of revenue can encourage suppliers to produce it. A planned system gives government decisions the main role in setting priorities and directing resources. A mixed system uses markets alongside public provision, ownership or regulation. These descriptions identify different organising arrangements; they do not prove that an outcome is good merely because it came through a market or a government decision. Start with the relevant problem, then ask whether the arrangement can solve it using the resources and information available.

blocks.heading: Follow a decision through the system
blocks.text: Consider an original example of additional transport services for an isolated community. Under market allocation, a private operator compares expected paying demand with its costs. A profitable route may attract an entrant, while a route with strong social need but little purchasing power may remain underserved. Under planned provision, the authority can prioritise access even when fares do not cover costs. It must still obtain vehicles, workers and funds, and decide which other services will receive fewer resources. A mixed arrangement could use private operation with a publicly supported service obligation. Calling the arrangement mixed is not enough: identify who decides the route, who pays, who operates the vehicles and how performance is checked. The important comparison is the ability of the actual arrangement to meet the stated access objective.

blocks.heading: Advantages need conditions
blocks.text: Competition can encourage a business to control costs and respond to customers, because dissatisfied buyers may choose another supplier. This incentive is weaker where customers lack alternatives or information. Market allocation can also leave benefits to third parties outside the buyer's and seller's calculations. Government action may improve access or take wider effects into account, but an authority can make mistakes if it lacks information or if performance is poorly monitored. A useful evaluation therefore compares arrangements against criteria such as efficiency, access, consumer choice and responsiveness. It explains why a benefit could occur and what could prevent it. Do not treat equal access as costless or assume that profit-seeking prevents a business from providing a useful service. The organisation of incentives and resources matters.

blocks.heading: Distinguish a supervisor from the entrepreneur
blocks.text: A supervisor employed for a salary contributes planning and coordination as part of labour. The entrepreneur's role concerns organising the business venture and bearing its business risk. Someone who starts a workshop may also repair products and supervise staff, so that individual supplies more than one type of contribution. Classify the role described in the particular situation rather than assuming that every person who gives instructions is the entrepreneur. Similarly, a payment into a bank account is not itself a new machine. It may provide finance for later productive investment, but the distinction between financing a resource and adding the productive resource remains important. Compare a deposit transfer with buying additional production equipment when testing this boundary.

blocks.heading: Build a judgement from the problem
blocks.text: The choice between arrangements depends on the economic problem and the available means of addressing it. Ask whether users can pay, whether alternative suppliers exist, whether costs and quality can be observed and how wider effects will be handled. A conclusion might favour market provision for a service with informed customers and active competition, but support a public role where essential access is otherwise missing. Explain the condition rather than labelling an entire system superior for every purpose. Topic 2.1 develops ownership forms; topic 3.2 develops market prices; topic 6.3 develops intervention. Here, preserve the distinction between the productive resources used and the system that coordinates their use. Financing and ownership can also differ: an authority might fund a privately operated service without owning the operator. Separate the payment arrangement from the decisions about production when identifying the system.
